title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2: Augustine restricts vivifying grace to the predestined and purpose-called — De grat. Christi 12–13; De praedest. sanct. 9; faith a gift to some not all
pass_a_gloss: But let us see what was the Orthodox sentence concerning this matter. From Augustine we have almost infinite testimonies. Excellent is that, De gratia Christi contra Pelag. et Caelestium, cap. 12. and 13. This grace whereby strength is perfected in weakness leads the predestinated and those called according to purpose unto the highest perfection and glorification. This grace God pours in more deeply and inwardly with ineffable sweetness, not only through those who plant and water outwardly, but also through himself, who secretly ministers his increase, so that he not only shows the truth, but also imparts charity. By these words he restricts this grace unto the predestinated and those called according to purpose, and at once shows that it is not efficacious from the event only, but from the purpose of the giver, and from the nature of the grace given. That such grace is not given unto all is clearer than noonday light. No less illustrious is that other testimony, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 8. Faith begun and perfected is God’s gift: and that this gift is given unto certain, not given unto certain, let him by no means doubt who wills not to contradict the most manifest sacred letters.
pass_b_english: What was the Orthodox view? From Augustine we have almost endless witnesses. Excellent is De gratia Christi contra Pelagium et Caelestium 12–13: This grace whereby strength is perfected in weakness leads the predestined and those called according to purpose to the highest perfection and glorification. God pours this grace in more deeply and inwardly with unspeakable sweetness—not only through those who plant and water outwardly, but through himself, who secretly gives the increase—so that he not only shows the truth but imparts charity. So he restricts this grace to the predestined and purpose-called, and shows it is efficacious not from the event alone but from the giver’s purpose and the nature of the grace given. That such grace is not given to all is clearer than noon. No less clear is De praedestinatione sanctorum 8: Faith begun and perfected is God’s gift; and that this gift is given to some and not to others, let no one doubt who will not contradict the plainest Scripture.
source_text: Sed videamus quae fuerit hac de re Orthodoxorum sententia. Ex Augustino habemus infinita paene testimonia. Praeclarum est illud, De gratia Christi contra Pelag. et Caelestium, cap. 12. et 13. Haec gratia qua virtus in infirmitate perficitur, praedestinatos et secundum propositum vocatos ad summam perfectionem glorificationisque perducit. Hanc gratiam Deus altius et interius cum ineffabili suavitate infundit, non solum per eos qui plantant et rigant extrinsecus, sed etiam per seipsum, qui incrementum suum ministrat occultus, ita ut non ostendat tantummodo veritatem, verum etiam impertiat charitatem. Hisce verbis hanc gratiam ad praedestinatos et secundum propositum vocatos restringit, atque simul ostendit, non esse efficacem ex eventu solummodo, sed ex proposito dantis, et ex ipsa datae gratiae natura. Talem gratiam omnibus non dari, meridiana luce clarius est. Non minus illustre est illud alterum testimonium, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 8. Fides inchoata et perfecta donum Dei est: et hoc donum quibusdam dari, quibusdam non dari, omnino non dubitet qui non vult manifestissimis sacris literis repugnare.
